findings.title: selectedTab has three uncoordinated direct-mutation sites, violating the single-owner HR-1 rule the residual claims to satisfy
findings.why_it_matters: The reducer/intent architecture exists specifically to guarantee that every runtime-significant fact has one coordinated writer, so state transitions are deterministic and auditable. selectedTab defeats that guarantee: it is writable from a two-way TabView binding plus two other classes' direct property assignment, so if two writers fire in overlapping windows (e.g. a deep link arrives while LoginViewModel.onSuccess is completing) the resulting tab depends on write order, not on intended navigation semantics.
findings.what_is_wrong: The residual's evidence was a doc-comment on NavigationStore (single owner per HR-1), not an inspection of who writes the field. The source shows selectedTab mutated directly from three independent owning types: TabView's binding (1), DeepLinkRouter.handle (2), and LoginViewModel.onSuccess (3) - none of these dispatch through an intent/reducer; they are unmediated @Published writes. That is a multiple-mutable-owner structure, the exact condition HR-1 prohibits.
findings.why_weakens_submission: This is the specific hollow-compliance failure mode a challenger is meant to catch: the residual's acceptance rationale verified what the documentation asserts, not what the code does, and the documentation is wrong. Letting this residual stand at 9.5 lets an unverified rule-compliance claim justify a HALT_SUCCESS promotion in the exact dimension it misrepresents.
findings.minimal_correction_path: Introduce a single reducer/intent entry point that owns all writes to selectedTab (e.g. store.dispatch(.selectTab(.library))), and change DeepLinkRouter.handle and LoginViewModel.onSuccess to dispatch intents instead of assigning nav.selectedTab directly; route the TabView binding through the same dispatch. This deletes two of the three direct-mutation code paths rather than relocating them, collapsing three independent owners into one.

findings.title: Deadline/polling infrastructure is generic and misclassified as irreducible vendor SDK surface
findings.why_it_matters: The accepted residual's entire justification for keeping VendorCatalogClient at 979 LOC and suppressing file_length rests on the claim that all of its content is essential, non-duplicable vendor-SDK surface area. If a meaningful portion is actually vendor-agnostic generic infrastructure, the 'irreducible' premise is false and the residual was accepted without first being properly minimized.
findings.what_is_wrong: The residual's own enumeration of the file's sections lists '100ms progress poll' and 'deadline-bounded timeout' alongside genuinely vendor-specific concerns (catalog search, playback control, vendor-error-code diagnosis). A poll-until-condition-or-deadline mechanism is a standard, vendor-agnostic concurrency primitive - it needs only a closure/predicate and a duration, not the vendor SDK's types or API shape. Unlike the error-code mapping (irreducibly bound to the vendor's specific codes) or the catalog/playback calls (bound to the vendor's specific SDK methods), this logic has no dependency on the vendor at all, yet it is currently only testable through the vendor-specific Test* fakes the report describes.
findings.why_weakens_submission: This directly falsifies the stated SPT rejection rationale ('Its size is the SDK surface area... not duplicated logic'): at least part of the size is not SDK surface area, it is generic infrastructure inlined into a vendor-specific file. The residual acceptance treated the file as an atomic, undecomposable unit when it demonstrably is not, so the 9.5 architecture_quality score with this residual was granted on an unminimized residual.
findings.minimal_correction_path: Extract the poll-until-deadline mechanism into a small, vendor-agnostic generic utility (e.g. a poll(interval:deadline:condition:) helper operating on closures/durations only), unit-testable with a trivial fake clock/condition and zero dependency on the vendor SDK or its Test* fakes. VendorCatalogClient calls this utility with its vendor-specific parameters (100ms interval, its deadline value) but no longer owns the polling/timeout mechanism itself. This shrinks the vendor-specific file and makes timeout/poll behavior independently testable.
